15.1 Double Integrals over Rectangles

The first lecture of Chapter 15. The volume of the solid under and above a rectangle is built the way Calc II built area: cut, approximate with boxes, add, take a limit. Then the tools that make it computable: iterated integrals, Fubini’s Theorem, products , and the average value of on .

4Which functions are integrable, and volume as a double integral

The limit in the definition exists for a large class of functions, including some with jumps.

Theorem (as stated on the board)

As long as is bounded on , and is continuous on , except possibly on a finite number of smooth curves, is integrable.

Beside it, a sketch: a surface over a region of the plane, with a green curve across it where the surface breaks, labelled “: a smooth curve”, and vertical hatching down to the floor.

At the bottom left of the board, the one-variable version: a graph with breaks in it between and (vertical lines in red at and ), and under it “” (partly hidden behind the instructor’s head in the photo).

Definition

Volume of over

Explanation (added)

“Integrable” means the limit of the double Riemann sums exists. A jump along a curve does not spoil it: the only boxes affected are those whose small rectangles touch , and those rectangles cover less and less area as (a smooth curve has no area). Since is bounded, those boxes also have bounded heights, so their total volume goes to . The 1-D picture is the same idea: a jump at a point affects only one strip, whose width goes to 0. The definition of volume uses the assumption from Section 2; if dips below the plane the double integral is still defined, but it counts volume below the -plane as negative (Section 9).

Continued at the top left of the next photo (Original image 16, beside Section 9), in green; the first word is cut off by the edge of the photo and reads like “and so”:

Explanation (added)

This is the Calc II “volume by slicing” formula . Freeze : the plane at that cuts the solid in a flat region under the curve , . Its area is a one-variable integral in : that is exactly the inner integral from Section 6. Adding up the slices, , gives the volume. Slicing the other way (freeze ) gives the same solid, so the same volume, which is the picture behind Fubini’s Theorem. The theorem itself says more: the two orders agree for any meeting its conditions, even where is negative.

A(x) = ∫₀² 3x y² dy = 8x = 8 · 2.50 = 20.00∫₁ˣ A(t) dt = 4x² − 4 = 21.000volume = ∫₁⁴ 8x dx = 60

In the plane x = 2.50 the solid’s cross-section is the region under the parabola z = 3(2.50)y². Its area A(x) = 8x grows in step with x, because x is just a constant factor in 3xy². Adding up these areas from x = 1 to x = 2.50 gives 21.000.

Explanation (added) · what an answer of 0 means

An answer of 0 does not mean there is no solid. Here is not on : the surface rises above the -plane where and dips below it where . The double integral counts volume above the plane as positive and volume below as negative, and for this the two are equal. The right-hand picture shows the same cancellation slice by slice: the slices for have positive net area, those for negative.

What a typical exam question looks like
  1. Estimate with a double Riemann sum. Given , , , and where the sample points go (upper-right corners, lower-left corners, or midpoints), compute and the sum by hand, and possibly say whether it is too big or too small (Section 3).
  2. Evaluate an iterated integral, or evaluate it in both orders and confirm the answers match (Sections 6–8).
  3. Choose the easier order. An integrand like or where one order is a substitution and the other needs integration by parts (Section 9).
  4. Evaluate by geometry. Recognise the solid (part of a ball, half a cylinder, a box or a wedge) and use a volume formula instead of integrating (Section 5).
  5. A product g(x)h(y) on a rectangle: split into two single integrals (Section 10).
  6. Volume of the solid under a surface and above a rectangle, or the average value of on a rectangle (Sections 8 and 11).

Tests are written without a calculator, so answers stay exact, like , or .

What a double integral measures

7. The board found on . Does that mean the region between the surface and has no volume? When does equal a volume?

Show the answer

No. is a volume only when on (Sections 4 and 8). Here is positive on part of and negative on another part (the hyperbolas and separate them, Section 9). The integral is the volume above the -plane minus the volume below it, and those two are equal. The total volume between the surface and would be , which is positive.
